claims.text: Applying deep cryogenic treatment after laser additive manufacturing will improve the tensile ductility of HfZrTiTa0.53.
Deep cryogenic treatment will increase the uniform tensile elongation of HfZrTiTa0.53 by at least 15%, from an assumed value near 13.5% to at least about 15.5%.
Deep cryogenic treatment will preserve the yield strength of HfZrTiTa0.53 within 10% of its baseline value.
Deep cryogenic treatment will preserve the impact-triggered chemical-energy release of HfZrTiTa0.53.
Laser-melting-deposited HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive yield strength of 786 MPa.
Laser-melting-deposited HfZrTiTa0.53 has a maximum compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
Laser-melting-deposited HfZrTiTa0.53 has approximately 13.5% terminal strain in compression.
Tensile-ductility data for HfZrTiTa0.53 are limited.
The proposed treatment consists of immersion in liquid nitrogen at approximately -196 °C for 24–48 hours.
Deep cryogenic treatment will induce or increase lattice distortion in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Deep cryogenic treatment may induce a phase transition in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Deep cryogenic treatment may form nanoscopic twin boundaries in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Deep cryogenic treatment will uniformly increase the residual stresses accumulated during laser melting deposition of HfZrTiTa0.53.
Twin formation and symmetry breaking will provide additional active slip systems in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The additional active slip systems will increase uniform elongation under tensile loading.
In laser-melting-deposited Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr, deep cryogenic treatment increased final tensile strength by 11% and elongation by 10% relative to the as-deposited state.
The proposed mechanical-testing domain is room temperature and a quasi-static strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1, excluding elevated-temperature and high-strain-rate validity.
The hypothesis will be tested by matched untreated and cryogenically treated groups using tensile, compression, and impact-triggered penetration tests.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant elongation increase of at least 15% while retaining yield strength within 10% and comparable impact-energy release will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% value is identified as terminal strain measured in compression but is then used as though it were the baseline uniform tensile elongation from which a 15% tensile improvement can be calculated.

The numerical baseline yield strength is compressive, whereas the prediction and falsification rule refer generically to retaining yield strength and include tensile yield strength; no separate tensile baseline is given.
Laser melting deposition is described as an example of conventional processing in the initial-state field but as laser additive manufacturing elsewhere.
